properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — Anthony, 2026-08-31, thinking out loud after the fork discussion. Nothing chosen.

HIS WORDS: "overarching requirements (not tied to implementation) and derived requirements that are dependent upon the design choices you make (things like, because you made decision X, this causes a requirement on capability Z). the overarching requirements are more like KPPs that are independent of design choices... do we need different tiers of requirements?"

═══ ⭐⭐ THE TIERS ALREADY EXIST, AND THE SCHEMA DEFINES THEM IN HIS OWN TERMS ═══
`Requirement.lineage`, declared and INDEXED in schema/core.yaml, values `[original, decomposed, derived]`:
· `original` — "the stakeholder's own word"
· `decomposed` — "a 1:1 split of a parent adding no new information — it DECOMPOSES that parent, and satisfying every child satisfies it"
· `derived` — "technical necessity nobody asked for, CREATED BY A DESIGN DECISION — it is GOVERNED_BY that Decision, and IF THE DECISION IS RE-OPENED THE REQUIREMENT MAY LOSE ITS REASON TO EXIST"

And the overarching tier exists as its own thing: a KPP is `Constraint.category = kpp`, carrying `limit` as the THRESHOLD and `objective` as the desired value — "inviolable intent, in the acquisition sense — a threshold that, if missed, fails the effort regardless of how well everything else went." Modelled as a Constraint subtype rather than a node type ON HIS OWN CALL, 2026-07-25, because the quantity/limit/direction triple and the budget rollup already existed. Two detectors read it: `KppUnbound` and a threshold-violation rule, and its violations rank above ordinary gaps.

═══ 🛑 MEASURED 2026-08-31, AND THIS IS THE FINDING ═══
    Requirements        205
      lineage=original  205   ← ALL of them, and `original` is the schema DEFAULT
      lineage=decomposed  0
      lineage=derived     0
    Constraints           4   all category=technical
      category=kpp        0
    Readers of Requirement.lineage: NONE. The only code mentions are in the setter.

⇒ THE VOCABULARY IS NOT MISSING. IT IS UNUSED AND UNREAD. Eighth instance today of a typed distinction built, an instruction that can set it, and no computation reading it.

⚠️ AND THE DEFAULT MAKES A CLAIM NOBODY MADE. `original` means "the stakeholder's own word". It is stamped on all 205 because nobody classified them, so the design currently asserts that every requirement came from a stakeholder — the same failure `Interface.designation` documents about itself ("BECAUSE it is the default, `internal` cannot distinguish 'deliberately internal' from 'nobody classified this'"), except here the default is the CLAIMY value rather than the neutral one.

═══ ⭐⭐ AND HIS TWO QUESTIONS TODAY ARE ONE QUESTION ═══
The schema already states the consequence that makes forks tractable: a derived requirement "is GOVERNED_BY that Decision, and if the decision is RE-OPENED the requirement may lose its reason to exist."

NOTHING COMPUTES THAT. And it is exactly what an exploration fork needs to be safe: reversing decision X in a fork should tell you which requirements lose their basis. Without it, a fork silently keeps requirements whose only reason was the choice it just reversed — which is the "reversals of previously settled requirements" worry he opened the fork discussion with.

⇒ SO THE TIERS ARE NOT A SEPARATE TOPIC FROM THE FORK. `lineage: derived` + GOVERNED_BY is the substrate that makes "what does this fork retire?" a computation instead of a judgement, and it is 0% populated.

═══ THE OPTIONS, none chosen ═══
① POPULATE NOTHING, BUILD NOTHING. The tiers are honest as unused vocabulary; a design where every requirement really is the stakeholder's word loses nothing. ⚠️ But this design is not that — several requirements here plainly exist because of a decision.
② FIX THE DEFAULT so unset is distinguishable from `original`. Cheapest thing that could not be wrong, and it stops the graph asserting stakeholder provenance for 205 requirements nobody classified. ⚠️ A schema default change, with the same reader question the `constrains`/`basis` item raised this morning.
③ BUILD THE READER — "which requirements lose their reason if this decision is re-opened?" — a traversal of GOVERNED_BY from a Decision to its derived requirements. ⭐ This is the fork-enabling one, and it needs ② or a population pass first or it returns nothing.
④ POPULATE `lineage` ON THIS DESIGN as a trial, to see whether the distinction is even discoverable in retrospect. ⚠️ Retro-classifying 205 requirements is a judgement call per node, and getting it wrong writes a false provenance claim.
⑤ A DETECTOR: a Requirement with `lineage: derived` and no GOVERNED_BY is a claim with no basis. Cheap, and it only fires once ④ happens.

⚠️ COUNTER-ARGUMENTS. (1) `dec:edge-orthogonality`'s test cuts both ways: a distinction earns its keep only if a computation reads it — so the honest reading of 0 readers is that the tiers have NOT earned their keep yet, and building a reader to justify a property is backwards. (2) KPPs at 0 of 4 may be correct for this project: reflow2 has no threshold whose miss fails the effort, and inventing one to exercise the vocabulary would be worse than leaving it empty. (3) Nobody has asked for tiering except in this conversation — no field report mentions it.
properties.name: OPEN — do we need requirement tiers? They exist, are better specified than the question assumes, and are 0% used — and the derived tier is what would make a design fork computable
properties.rationale: Recorded under the brainstorm discipline — ideas as ideas, nothing promoted. The measurement is the part worth keeping whatever is decided: the tiers Anthony is describing are already declared, in his own vocabulary, and are 0% populated with no reader. That reframes the question from 'do we need this?' to 'why has something already built never been reached for?', which is the eighth instance of that shape recorded today.
